title: Carnival ball audiences and how they danced ragtime
summary: White carnival audiences loved anything the band played; Laine explains they danced two-steps to ragtime, not waltzes.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: All right. Now, what song did these white people at the carnival balls used to like the most that you played? Which song did they like the most? Most Anything and Everything. There wasn't one particular song they liked?
No. No. No. Well, none in particular. I see. None in particular. In fact, they didn't care what we played. I don't care how we played it or what we played. We got a big hand.
Why was that, do you think? Why did they like you? Why did they like you? Why did you get those big hands?

I don't know. I have no idea. I don't know. They must have liked the music. Could be. They must have liked the music. Otherwise, they wouldn't clap like they did in hollering and whistling and clap on the phone. All that sort of stuff. Play it over.
Now, did these people used to dance to that ragtime music? Yes. Is it back in the 1880s? In the 1880s? They used to dance with it. How did they dance? Was it kind of a waltz or a...

No, in all kinds. Two steps, shutters, and all like that. Uh-huh. Yeah. But they danced with each other. They didn't dance by themselves. They couldn't dance that stuff with a waltz. I see. See? Two steps. A waltz is different times. Right. See? Six, eight, something like that, you know. See? A different time. Right. They can't dance no ragtime music with a waltz. You couldn't even play ragtime with a waltz.
